title: Townsville was going to be a cyber security hub. What happened?
snippet: Updated 14 September 2026: this article has been split in two and tightened to a strict primary-source standard. The current landscape (training, jobs, commercial providers and what’s missing today...
content: Updated 14 September 2026: this article has been split in two and tightened to a strict primary-source standard. The current landscape (training, jobs, commercial providers and what’s missing today) now has its own companion piece: Cyber security in Townsville: training, jobs, businesses and what is missing.In June 2020, governments announced that Townsville would join Australia’s national network of cyber security innovation nodes. Six years later, I wanted to know what became of that specific, named initiative: not cyber security in North Queensland generally, but the funded program itself.This is deliberately a narrow piece. I have only included claims I can trace to a primary source: a Council announcement, a government publication, an organisation’s own statement, an archived job listing. Where the trail runs out, I say so rather than guess at what filled the gap.What was announcedThe joint Commonwealth and Queensland announcement on 2 June 2020 proposed Cyber Security Innovation Nodes in Brisbane, Townsville and the Sunshine Coast, delivered by AustCyber in partnership with the Queensland Government and the two regional councils.Townsville City Council’s announcement the following day, under then-Mayor Jenny Hill, said the node would put Townsville “at the forefront” of cyber capability development, give local businesses access comparable with the capital cities, and sit alongside Smart Precinct NQ and the North Queensland Regional Data Centre. Council specifically pointed to the Certificate IV in Cyber Security at TAFE Queensland’s Pimlico campus as a training pathway.On 17 March 2021, Council announced the node had launched and its inaugural manager had been appointed. The stated next steps were training opportunities, forums, seminars, and cyber security health checks for local businesses.That gives a clear set of commitments to measure against: people trained, businesses helped, relationships built, a healthier local security posture.The role itself was realIt’s worth being specific about what “the node” actually was, because press releases can make an initiative sound more abstract than it was.AustCyber’s own job listing for the role, archived by the Wayback Machine in November 2020, since removed from AustCyber’s current site, describes a genuine, funded position: a two-year AustCyber contract, 15 to 22.5 hours a week, $120,000–$145,000 pro rata. Its responsibilities included establishing an industry advisory group, delivering cyber security events across North Queensland, and (this line matters) “maintain[ing] node activities and deliverables within budgetary and resource constraints and meet[ing] evaluation and reporting requirements.”AustCyber itself expected reporting against outcomes. I have not found that reporting published anywhere.Smart Precinct NQ and the cyber node were different thingsThe organisations and projects in this story are easily collapsed into a single “cyber hub.” That makes the funding story harder to understand, and it’s worth being precise here because the two are frequently confused.Smart Precinct NQ was a broader innovation and entrepreneurship organisation. Its work covered business development, founders, mentoring and connections between industry, government and research. The cyber node was a specific, separately funded initiative operating within that wider environment.AustCyber’s August 2021 submission to Home Affairs explains the national funding model: most of AustCyber’s funding came from Commonwealth grants, with contractual arrangements with state governments and with Townsville and Sunshine Coast councils, matched by AustCyber to deliver the node network. That establishes participation by all three levels of government, without supplying a separate Townsville total.The 2019 Townsville City Deal progress report records SPNQ’s incorporation and a $1.5 million Townsville City Council commitment to support business growth and investment. Queensland’s Regional Enablers recipients list separately records $298,986 for SPNQ’s NQ Regional Enablers Program, focused on sustainability and circular-economy innovation.Neither figure is a stand-alone budget for the Townsville cyber node. Public record What the amount relates to What it establishes 2019 City Deal report: $1.5 million Council commitment Smart Precinct NQ; business growth and investment A commitment to the broader organisation, not a statement of cyber-node expenditure. Regional Enablers award: $298,986 A sustainability and circular-economy innovation program Project funding for a defined purpose, unrelated to cyber security. AustCyber job listing: $120,000–$145,000 pro rata One two-year node manager contract The cost of a single role, not the node’s total budget. Adding these figures together would not produce a reliable total for “money spent on Townsville cyber security.” I have not established a separate, reconciled Townsville node budget from the sources reviewed for this article. That is a gap worth addressing, particularly if governments want the community to assess what the investment achieved.Then the trail goes coldTownsville was still being counted as an active node as late as 2022: Stone & Chalk’s Australia’s Cyber Security Sector Competitiveness Plan 2022 states that “three Cyber Security Innovation nodes have been established in Queensland since June 2020; in Brisbane, Townsville and the Sunshine Coast.”After that, the Department of Industry’s account of the Industry Growth Centres Initiative sets out the relevant dates: AustCyber merged with Stone & Chalk in February 2021, AustCyber’s contract with the Australian Government ended in June 2024, and the wider Industry Growth Centres program ended on 31 December 2024. The department lists a national network of innovation nodes among AustCyber’s former activities.None of that establishes a Townsville-specific closure date, or tells us whether the node’s local functions (the advisory group, the events, the health checks) continued under a different arrangement, were formally wound up, or simply stopped without an announcement. I have not found a close-out evaluation, a handover notice, or any public reconciliation of what the node delivered against its 2021 commitments.One thing is worth separating out clearly, because it’s easy to conflate. Smart Precinct NQ went through its own, later wind-down: its former chief executive publicly said in 2026 that its operational grant funding would not be renewed, and SPNQ itself subsequently confirmed that its public programs and events had concluded after a final event on 24 June 2026. That is a 2026 event affecting a different, broader organisation. It should not be read as evidence of when the Townsville cyber node itself stopped operating. By the evidence above, that had already faded from public view years earlier. The companion article to this one covers what SPNQ’s closure means for the current landscape.Four questions the public record doesn’t answer What happened to the Townsville node’s functions after AustCyber’s Commonwealth contract ended in 2024? What funding was allocated and spent specifically on the node, and what outcomes were recorded against the “evaluation and reporting requirements” AustCyber itself specified? Was the node ever formally closed or handed over, and if so, to whom? Did the training, forums and business health checks promised in March 2021 actually happen, and at what scale?Where this leaves thingsI’m not concluding that the Townsville Cyber Security Innovation Node failed. I don’t have the evidence to say that, and an absent report is not proof that the work didn’t happen; it may have occurred and simply left a poor public trail.What I can say is that a publicly funded regional initiative, backed by three levels of government and specific enough to have its own job description and budget, does not have a public record six years later that lets a resident answer basic questions about what it delivered. That is the part of this story that remains unresolved, and it’s a fair thing to ask Council, the Queensland Government and whoever now holds AustCyber’s records to fix.For what cyber security in Townsville actually looks like today (training, jobs, commercial providers, and what a coordinating role might still be missing), see the companion piece: Cyber security in Townsville: training, jobs, businesses and what is missing. For businesses that want practical help right now, I’ve also written a guide on Suburban Secure: Where can Townsville small businesses get cyber security help?Disclosure: I founded Suburban Secure and provide commercial technology and security advice through it. That is one part of the local service market. The publicly funded coordination and industry-development role discussed here has a broader purpose than any individual consultancy.BibliographyPublic sources were checked on 14 September 2026. This article is based on documentary research; it does not include interviews or direct confirmation from Council, AustCyber, SPNQ or TAFE. Only claims I could trace to a primary source are included.Andrews, K., & Jones, K. (2020, June 2). AustCyber nodes strengthen QLD cyber economy [Joint ministerial media release]. Australian Government.Townsville City Council. (2020, June 3). Cyber security node for Townsville.Townsville City Council. (2021, March 17). Cyber security hub launched, manager appointed.AustCyber. (2020, November). AustCyber Cyber Security Innovation Node Manager (QLD - Townsville based position) [Job listing; archived via the Wayback Machine, since removed from AustCyber’s current site]. Retrieved 14 September 2026.AustCyber. (2021, August). Response to the Strengthening Australia’s cyber security regulations and incentives discussion paper, p. 5 [Submission to Home Affairs; funding and node-network arrangements].Australian Government, Queensland Government, & Townsville City Council. (n.d.). Townsville City Deal: Annual progress report 2019, p. 9. Accessed 14 September 2026.Queensland Government. (2024, September 30). Regional Enablers recipients. Advance Queensland.Stone & Chalk / AustCyber. (2022). Australia’s Cyber Security Sector Competitiveness Plan 2022, p. 68 [Lists Townsville as one of three Queensland Cyber Security Innovation Nodes established since June 2020].Department of Industry, Science and Resources. (n.d.). Industry Growth Centres Initiative ends. Accessed 14 September 2026.Cazzulino, C. (2026). A personal update: Departure from Smart Precinct NQ and operational funding [LinkedIn post]. Accessed 14 September 2026.Smart Precinct NQ. (2026). Company updates [LinkedIn posts: final event on 24 June, and subsequent conclusion of public programs]. Accessed 14 September 2026.

title: Nicholas Townsville: now I'm competing with a brewery
snippet: On 27 August, I wrote about the problem with being called Nick in Townsville. Search for Nick Townsville and I found myself looking at Nick Dametto, while trying to convince Google that there was a...
content: On 27 August, I wrote about the problem with being called Nick in Townsville. Search for Nick Townsville and I found myself looking at Nick Dametto, while trying to convince Google that there was another local Nick worth finding.Today, I tried the full version of my name.Nicholas Townsville.The first result I saw was Selwyn Nicholas Brewing Co.Apparently, adding four letters has taken my personal SEO experiment from local politics to craft beer.On my first check today, 12 September 2026, this website appeared to be around fourth for that search. That is a starting observation from the results I saw, rather than a position I can claim everyone will see. Still, it was enough to make me wonder: could nickosullivan.id.au eventually get ahead of Selwyn Nicholas for Nicholas Townsville?I have a website, a surname and years of working in technology around Townsville. They have beer.I can see why this might be a difficult marketing exercise.An unlikely beer correspondentI am not typically much of a drinker, and I have not tried a Selwyn Nicholas brew. My discovery of the brewery came through a search result, so I cannot offer tasting notes or tell you which one to order.I am, however, known to not mind a Great Northern Super Crisp from time to time.That probably tells you roughly how sophisticated my beer commentary is going to be. I am much more comfortable discussing a network configuration than explaining what the hops are doing.There is something amusing about researching a local brewery because it has a stronger claim to your first name in Google. Most people would probably start with what is on tap. I started with where they appeared in the results.A little background on Selwyn Nicholas Brewing CoThe brewery is at 365 Woolcock Street, Garbutt, near the Domain shopping precinct. According to its own website, the team converted an old gym into a microbrewery venue.That is quite a change of use for a building. I spend enough time thinking about how old technology can find a new purpose; apparently, the same principle can apply to somewhere that used to house exercise equipment.The Townsville North Queensland tourism listing describes Selwyn Nicholas as locally owned and independently operated, with a focus on traditional brewing techniques and a range of beer styles. The Independent Brewers Association welcomed it as a brewery member in March 2025.I would still like to hear the story behind the name itself. As a Nicholas currently trying to work out how to market his own name, I feel I have a fairly specific reason to be interested.For now, that gives me a much better picture of the business that appeared above me: a local independent brewery that has given an old space a new purpose, with its own place in Townsville and the wider brewing community.It also means I have now written about them and linked to their website while wondering how to move ahead of them.An excellent start to my competitive strategy.Marketing the right NicholasThe useful part of this little detour is how familiar the problem feels.Nicholas Townsville gives a search engine very little to go on. It could be someone trying to remember a person’s full name. It could also be someone who remembers part of a brewery’s name and the city it is in.Looking at the brewery’s website and local listings, I can understand why it would be a plausible result. That is my reading of the situation, though; I cannot see Google’s reasoning for the order it showed me.For my part, the introduction I want people to find is straightforward: I am Nicholas “Nick” O’Sullivan, a Townsville IT professional who writes about technology, cyber security and life in North Queensland. There is more about that on my About page.The challenge is making that connection clear wherever my work appears. Using Nicholas and Nick consistently, linking articles to the person behind them, and writing about things I actually know gives people a better chance of recognising the right result.There is room to have a bit of fun with it. I can take an interest in where my website ranks without treating every other Nicholas as a branding emergency. And if someone looking for a local beer discovers Selwyn Nicholas through this article, that seems a perfectly reasonable outcome too.Meanwhile, back at Nick TownsvilleThere has been little improvement so far in where nickosullivan.id.au appears for Nick Townsville. The original experiment is still running, and a fuller follow-up will come when there is more to report.It has only been a little over two weeks since that first article. Google’s SEO Starter Guide says changes can take anything from hours to several months to be reflected in Search, so this is still early days.I will add Nicholas Townsville to the searches I watch, alongside the more specific versions of my full name. Today’s apparent fourth place gives me something to record, and a later look at Search Console should be more useful than repeatedly refreshing one search.Getting ahead of the brewery would make a funny update. Helping somebody who has heard my name through work or around Townsville actually find me would be useful every day.Until then, Selwyn Nicholas has given me another story to tell, and possibly a reason to broaden my beer research one day.For now, I will keep working on the website. The occasional Great Northern Super Crisp can stay an occasional Great Northern Super Crisp.I had hoped using my full name might make this easier. I had not accounted for the Nicholas with a taproom.27 September 2026: There is now a follow-up with search screenshots and the first month of numbers. The brewery is still ahead in my latest “Nicholas Townsville” screenshot, but the original article is appearing directly below it.

title: School marketing in the age of AI: do we need students' faces?
tags: education, privacy, artificial-intelligence, governance, marketing, social-media, queensland
snippet: Schools should be able to celebrate learning while exposing less of children’s identities online. My view is that an identifiable face in public school marketing should need a clear, documented pur...
content: Schools should be able to celebrate learning while exposing less of children’s identities online. My view is that an identifiable face in public school marketing should need a clear, documented purpose, with consent and a considered assessment of the exposure involved.That matters for independent schools, Catholic schools and state schools across Queensland and Australia. It also deserves attention from sporting clubs, charities and other organisations that feature children in promotional imagery.The question is whether the value of publishing an identifiable photograph justifies the exposure we create for the person in it. A signed photo consent form is part of that decision. It cannot prevent someone else copying or manipulating an image.On 28 July 2026, the eSafety Commissioner published advice on sharing school imagery in the age of AI. It describes rising reports of school-related image misuse, including sexualised deepfakes and abuse targeting staff. Between January and March 2026, eSafety received more than 100 reports about anonymous accounts targeting schools and staff; almost all involved imagery taken from school websites or social media.The advisory recommends reviewing image-sharing practices. Posting fewer images, or none, can reduce exposure, although it cannot eliminate misuse. Its advice is to assess purpose, consent, audience and identifying details before publication.This advisory does not announce a federal ban on school photographs. eSafety explains that it can act against certain harmful material under the Online Safety Act, including issuing removal notices for image-based abuse, but some harmful content falls outside its legal thresholds. Schools have good reason to act before relying on a later takedown.Creating sexualised images of children is an abusive use of AI. The responsibility belongs to those who create and circulate that material. Schools can still make considered decisions about the images they make available.In its 11 September report, 7NEWS said Tyndale Christian School Group had stopped publishing identifiable student photographs on public social media. Tyndale described a proactive privacy and digital-safety review, with no single incident prompting the decision.St Hilda’s Anglican School for Girls in Western Australia announced its approach on 27 January 2026: avoiding clearly identifiable student images on public social media, with alternatives including side profiles, silhouettes, backs of heads and distant group shots. Hope Barr, the school’s Head of Marketing and Communications, explains that families can access a password-protected gallery, with downloads limited to images featuring their daughter.In Queensland, Brigidine College in Brisbane had also acted before July’s advisory. ABC News reported on 19 April 2026 that it had restricted recognisable student photographs and reduced images per post. Its approach included side profiles, group shots and photographs from behind. Principal Brendan Cahill linked the change to AI image-manipulation concerns; parental consent remained part of the process.That gives schools a useful distinction between communicating publicly and sharing family memories. Restricted access reduces the audience; recipients can still copy or reshare images, so expectations and access controls matter.Jacob Shultz’s earlier provocation about school marketing asked what happens when social media stops being the default. His suggestions included direct relationships through mailing lists, events and spaces schools can manage more carefully.A school can explain its teaching, show student projects, invite families onto campus and communicate its values without a steady stream of identifiable children’s portraits.A playful back-to-school concept using animals. Clearly fictional illustrations can give a campaign personality without exposing a child’s identity.The animal classroom illustrations here make that point with some humour. Other options include hands building a project, artwork with names removed, equipment and spaces. A photograph taken from behind or side-on may tell the story with less facial detail. Every composition still needs checking for recognisable features, names and context. Staff participation deserves the same consideration.The sideways-turn advice has a research basis. Yisroel Mirsky’s 2022 DF-Captcha preprint proposed head turns and other challenges to expose live deepfakes. Its preliminary experiments showed visible defects when challenging the tested facial reenactment system. The paper identified difficulties generating poses and actions poorly represented in training data.These are historical tests of making a fake face follow a caller’s movements live. They do not measure whether a published profile photograph can support a convincing edited image, or establish a reliable detection trick for today’s systems. A side profile and a cropped frontal photograph also reveal different information.Rafay Baloch recommends considering abstract or partial-face profile images and limiting detailed facial imagery. That is precautionary advice; the post provides no comparative measurements of protection.Research at ICCV in 2017 already demonstrated generating frontal views from profile photographs while retaining identity cues. This does not guarantee accurate recovery of hidden details, but shows why a profile is not a dependable technical barrier.Schools can reduce unnecessary identifying material now and review their approach as technology changes. I have not found a validated percentage reduction in deepfake risk from a half-face crop; it should never become an automatic approval rule.I have seen the need for scrutiny first-hand. At a school that was not a state high school, I saw a certificate photograph exposing a student’s name and student number. I contacted the school privately, and it blurred the image. This shows how a celebratory post can disclose more than intended.On the few North Queensland state high school pages I have viewed, student images remain common. I have also noticed marketing and communications roles advertised in Queensland state schools. Those staff need clear expectations and leadership support.The Department of Education already has a social media promotion procedure covering consent, approvals, training and moderation. Its consent procedure requires consent to be voluntary, informed, specific and current.As at 12 September 2026, I could not find an explicit direction to stop identifiable student photographs because of AI deepfakes in those two public procedures or the department’s social media policy. That is a limited observation: the promotion procedure also links to employee-only guides that I could not review.I would welcome a formal recommendation from Australian education bodies, with independent school associations asking members to agree to a common framework and education departments providing equivalent direction. My preferred starting point would be to use identifiable faces only where necessary and justified, supported by: Photography briefs with examples staff can use immediately. An approval process that checks the whole image and caption, including certificates, badges and identifiers. Separate arrangements for public campaigns and restricted family sharing, with clear consent choices. A scheduled review of public archives, respecting applicable recordkeeping requirements. A named person responsible for training, concerns and responding to image misuse.A shared framework would give principals, boards and marketing staff an agreed position to explain to families. At the next marketing meeting, redesign one campaign to expose less of students’ identities, then record when identifiable imagery would be justified in the school’s publishing policy.

title: Australia's privacy reforms: what is changing and when
snippet: Australia’s privacy reforms now involve several different timelines. Some changes are already law, others have a December milestone, and the latest package remains an exposure draft. School leaders...
content: Australia’s privacy reforms now involve several different timelines. Some changes are already law, others have a December milestone, and the latest package remains an exposure draft. School leaders need to separate those categories to decide what requires action now.The Attorney-General’s Department opened consultation on the Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026 on 31 August. Submissions close on 18 September 2026, and the proposals remain subject to government consideration. Consultation details.This article explains the reform position. Its companion, How independent schools should govern technology approvals, sets out a practical process for turning supplier assessments into school decisions.Status checked on 12 September 2026. Lead photo by Philipp Katzenberger on Unsplash.What has happened, and what comes next Development Position as at 12 September 2026 First reform legislation Parliament passed the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 in November 2024, including the framework for a statutory privacy tort and the Children’s Online Privacy Code. Attorney-General’s Department. Serious invasions of privacy The statutory tort commenced on 10 June 2025, providing an additional avenue for redress through the courts. OAIC explanation. Automated decision transparency New privacy-policy obligations commence on 10 December 2026 for covered automated decision making. OAIC issues paper. Children’s Online Privacy Code The OAIC must register the final Code by 10 December 2026. Registration and the commencement of obligations are separate matters. OAIC consultation page. The 2026 exposure draft Consultation is open. The draft commencement table contains no dates, so this package has no settled start date. Exposure draft, clause 2. Independent schools should also establish their existing obligations. The OAIC says private schools are usually covered by the Privacy Act, including through turnover, related organisations or providing health services and holding health information. First aid and medication support can be relevant. Government schools generally operate under different arrangements. OAIC guidance on children and education.December deserves its own preparationThe automated-decision provisions concern programs that use personal information to make, or substantially and directly contribute to making, decisions expected to significantly affect a person’s rights or interests. Privacy policies must describe relevant categories of information and decisions. A human making the final decision does not automatically exclude the process. OAIC issues paper, pp. 12–15 and 25–26.I would begin by finding systems that score or recommend outcomes for admissions, scholarships, student interventions or recruitment. Those are review examples; whether the obligation applies depends on the actual process and statutory threshold. System owners will need to explain how software contributes before a privacy-policy update can accurately describe it.The Children’s Online Privacy Code needs separate attention. Its scope concerns specified online service providers likely to be accessed by children, with exceptions. Schools should assess their activities and suppliers against the final instrument and its transition arrangements. Having students alone does not settle coverage. OAIC background.What the new exposure draft proposesFair and reasonable information handlingThe draft would replace several collection, use and disclosure rules with a fair, reasonable and lawful handling requirement, subject to exceptions. Factors include expectations, transparency, minimisation, choice and proportional harm. Children’s best interests would be a primary consideration. Exposure draft, Schedule 2.For schools, my starting question would be whether each information request is justified by the activity. A broad enrolment consent should never end that assessment, particularly where students have little practical choice about participation.Broader definitions and clearer consent requirementsThe proposed personal-information definition includes information relating to identifiable people, with identifiers and behavioural patterns among its examples. Collection includes generating or deriving information. Defined precise geolocation tracking would become sensitive information. Exposure draft, Schedule 1.Consent would expressly need to be voluntary, informed, current, specific and unambiguous. Sensitive-information collection would generally continue to require consent, with exceptions. White & Case analysis.I would include learning profiles, device identifiers and app telemetry in school reviews alongside names and contact details. Removing a name may leave other information that identifies the student.The proposed changes would affect operational preparation as well as privacy documentation.A tighter breach-notification timetableThe proposal would give entities 72 hours to notify the Information Commissioner once they become aware of reasonable grounds to believe an eligible data breach has occurred. The existing requirement to take reasonable steps to complete a suspected eligible breach assessment within 30 days remains. Preparedness and harm-mitigation duties would also be strengthened. Consultation paper, Schedule 3.That trigger matters. An initial technical alert and awareness of grounds to believe an eligible breach occurred are different stages. Notification to affected people has its own requirements. Staff need prompt escalation pathways, while those assessing the incident need supplier cooperation and access to decision-makers.Responsibility for outsourced processingThe processor proposal applies where both parties are Australian Privacy Principle entities. A provider handling information under a controller’s written instructions could receive an exception from certain obligations, with relevant responsibility resting on the controller. Processors retain direct APP 1 and APP 11 duties; conduct outside instructions falls outside the exception. Consultation paper, Schedule 6.Schools would need to understand each provider’s role in the particular activity. Contracts should establish permitted handling, including whether the supplier uses information for its own analytics, advertising or AI training.Information holdings, security and disposalProposed APP 11 changes would require identification of relevant personal information, consideration of destruction when no longer needed, and regular evaluation of compliance. Legally required retention is protected. Exposure draft, Schedule 3.Preparation should connect the records policy to actual systems, exports and supplier accounts. Schools will need to account for applicable education, child-safety and other retention requirements when deciding what can be removed.What remains unsettledThe proposed erasure right targets large digital platforms. It is not a general right to demand deletion of every school record. Broader removal of the small-business and employee-records exemptions is outside this package. White & Case analysis.A proposed 60-day complaint-response requirement is among measures still being developed in the consultation paper, rather than fully expressed in the exposure draft. Consultation paper, pp. 38–40.Schools can use the consultation to explain implementation issues such as supplier contracts, record retention and the time needed to review existing systems. Meanwhile, leadership can assign an owner to the December preparation and start the technology assessment and approval work that already supports sound privacy governance.ReferencesGovernment reform documentsAttorney-General’s Department. (2026, August 31). Privacy reform: Consultation on exposure draft legislation [Closes 18 September 2026].Attorney-General’s Department. (2026). Exposure draft: Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026 [Draft legislation]. Accessible Word version.Attorney-General’s Department. (2026). Privacy reform: Consultation paper, particularly Schedules 3 and 6 and pp. 38–40.Attorney-General’s Department. (n.d.). Privacy [Reform overview]. Accessed 12 September 2026.Regulator guidanceOffice of the Australian Information Commissioner. (2025, June 19). Statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy.Office of the Australian Information Commissioner. (2026, May). Automated decision-making transparency obligation (APP 1): Issues paper.Office of the Australian Information Commissioner. (2026). Draft Children’s Online Privacy Code: Consultation for industry, civil society, academia; and OAIC releases exposure draft of the Children’s Online Privacy Code.Office of the Australian Information Commissioner. (n.d.). Children and young people. Accessed 12 September 2026.Legal analysisBoyle, N., Kermond, C., & Moore, A. (2026, September 8). Australia privacy update: Proposed privacy law reform. White & Case LLP.

title: How independent schools should govern technology approvals
snippet: Before a school deploys an app, someone should be able to explain what information it will handle, why it needs it, what has been checked and who has accepted the remaining risk. That decision shou...
content: Before a school deploys an app, someone should be able to explain what information it will handle, why it needs it, what has been checked and who has accepted the remaining risk. That decision should still be understandable when the people who made it have moved on.That is where I would start preparing for Australia’s proposed privacy reforms. A school needs a dependable way to turn evidence about a service into a decision about its use, then carry that decision through to the classroom.The 2026 exposure draft consultation closes on 18 September. The package remains a proposal, but the OAIC’s existing security guidance already addresses management oversight, information registers and supplier assessment. Schools can begin this work now. The separate privacy reform explainer covers what has happened, December’s milestones and what remains unsettled.The process I would build is:ST4S and supplier evidence → assessment of the school’s intended use → delegated approval and recorded conditions → consent where required before use → periodic review.An approved-service register should connect those steps. Its value is the decision it records and helps staff implement.Start with the assessment work education already hasSafer Technologies 4 Schools (ST4S) provides a substantial foundation. Education Services Australia administers it for participating government, Catholic and independent education sectors in Australia and New Zealand. Assessments cover privacy, security, interoperability and online safety. Suppliers submit responses and supporting evidence where required; the ST4S team analyses and validates them. Results reach schools through approved stakeholders. ST4S assessment process.I would use the relevant findings to inform a school’s assessment, checking the product, edition and assessment date. The local decision still needs to account for the students involved, enabled features, information supplied and proposed use. The same platform may present different risks in different configurations.Queensland’s Department of Education shows how review evidence can support everyday administration. On page 7 of its online-services consent guideline, Process: Obtaining consent, step 1 asks staff to gather each relevant service’s name, URL, hosting location, purpose, terms, privacy policy, information disclosed and additional consent requirements. It directs staff to an Online Service Risk Review, where available; those reviews are restricted to DoE employees. Consent guideline, page 7.Principals oversee the approved-service register, and incoming principals should review it and accept responsibility for continued use. Guideline, page 5.Independent schools can adapt that approach to their own structure and legal obligations. There is an established education-sector pattern to learn from: assess the service, make a decision, communicate its conditions and retain responsibility as staff change. The department’s specific consent rules belong to its own legal and policy framework.Build a register that records the decisionThe assessment needs to follow the information a product handles in its intended use. Photo by Vitaly Gariev on Unsplash.For a SaaS platform, third-party iOS app or software package, I would maintain a privacy and technology risk register with the fields below. These are suggested governance practices, not a template prescribed by the proposed legislation. Record What it should tell the school Service and purpose Supplier, product, edition, URL, school owner, student cohort and intended use. Include free apps and trials. Information and location Data collected or inferred; hosting, backup and support countries; subcontractors; advertising or AI-training uses. Evidence Dated privacy policy and relevant clauses, contract, processing terms, ST4S findings and outstanding questions. Separate supplier claims from verified evidence. Controls Access settings, data minimisation, incident reporting, retention and deletion arrangements. Reference restricted consent records where needed. Assessment and approval Likelihood and impact of harm, remaining risk, rationale, permitted use, conditions, decision status, approver and date. Review and exit Review date, changes that trigger reassessment, contract end date and responsibility for closing accounts or removing data. Keep decision status separate from the risk rating. A service can have a completed assessment and still be awaiting approval, deferred while questions are resolved, or declined. Staff need to know whether they may use it and under what conditions.Australian hosting alone cannot establish trustworthiness. Consider overseas support access, backups, subcontractors, contractual permissions and actual product behaviour. The OAIC’s APP 8 guidance explains the obligations and exceptions around overseas disclosure. A location label cannot answer all of those questions.Make approval responsibilities explicitA technical review may establish that an application works on managed devices and supports appropriate access controls. Educational suitability, privacy obligations, contractual commitments and acceptance of remaining risk each need an accountable decision as well.I would allocate the work this way, adapting the roles to the school’s size: IT coordinates evidence and assesses configuration, security, integrations and operational support. Educational, privacy and business leads assess the proposed use, student impact, consent requirements and contract. Seek legal advice where interpretation is needed. The principal or delegated executive approves use within agreed authority, recording conditions and the remaining risk. The board or its relevant committee oversees material risks and exceptions, according to the school’s governance arrangements.One person may hold several responsibilities in a smaller school. The record should still show which decisions they made and under what delegation. No approval can authorise unlawful handling.Work through the actual classroom useConsider a fictional reading app that requests a full date of birth, student voice recordings and persistent location access. The first assessment question is the educational need for each. Can the lesson work with an age band, shorter audio retention or location disabled?Suppose the supplier’s policy leaves AI training and audio deletion unclear. Record those gaps and defer approval for identified student recordings until they are resolved. If the school subsequently approves use, specify the cohort, configuration, information permitted, consent requirements and review date. A product name with a green rating would lose that context.Where consent is required, the process must reach the staff using the service. They need a workable way to check current consent before accounts are created or information is uploaded, and to act on withdrawals or changes. An alternative activity should be planned where participation depends on optional consent.I would keep individual consent records access-controlled and link them to the approved use. The general service register should give staff the instructions they need without exposing unnecessary student information.Keep the decision useful after rolloutA service approval also needs an owner for incidents, changes and eventual retirement.A new AI feature, changed privacy terms, acquisition or incident should trigger a review when it changes the assessed use or risk. Set a periodic review date as well, with shorter intervals for services handling more consequential information.I would test the process with a supplier breach reported on a Friday afternoon during school holidays. Can the register identify the service owner, affected information and supplier contact? Who can activate the response, obtain advice and authorise communications? Give those roles deputies so the response can operate when the principal or usual technical contact is unavailable.Retirement needs similar attention. Abandoned trials, historic class exports, old accounts and duplicate files can outlive the activity that created them. Apply the school’s approved retention requirements, including applicable education and child-safety obligations, and verify what happens to information in the provider’s systems when use ends. The OAIC’s Guide to securing personal information provides an existing foundation for this work.Future tools could compare supplier policies, flag changes and draft risk ratings. I would want every generated assessment to expose its evidence, assumptions and unknowns. A tool can help keep the register current; a named reviewer still needs to assess the result and a delegated decision-maker approve the use.Quick sheet for the next leadership meeting Focus A concrete next step Find the services Reconcile purchasing, device-management and sign-in records with staff declarations of free apps and trials. Establish ownership Nominate the privacy lead, service owners, approvers and escalation path. Start with consequential data Prioritise health, wellbeing, safeguarding, biometric and location information. Test the workflow Take one existing service through evidence, assessment, approval, consent checks and review scheduling. Make decisions usable Publish approved uses and conditions for staff; keep detailed assessments and student records appropriately restricted. Report what needs attention Bring unresolved questions, overdue reviews and material exceptions to leadership. Track the reform milestones alongside them. Ask for a reviewable decision on one service at the next meeting, with an owner and a date for extending the process. That makes progress visible and exposes where responsibilities or evidence are missing.Related work: the governance, risk and compliance services at Suburban Secure, which I founded, cover risk registers, policies and reporting to leadership.ReferencesEducation and assessment resourcesEducation Services Australia.
